summary: Most travelers must arrange a visa before arriving in the Republic of the Congo through a Congolese embassy or consulate, while fellow CEMAC citizens from Cameroon, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea, Chad and the Central African Republic enter freely.

payments.text: The Government of Canada says the economy is primarily cash-based. Major hotels and stores generally accept major credit cards, euros and US dollars (confirm when you book), but outside these establishments in Brazzaville and Pointe-Noire credit cards are rarely accepted.

safety.text: Opportunistic crime such as pickpocketing occurs, particularly in Brazzaville and Pointe-Noire, and criminals may target foreigners and vehicles, especially outside towns and in the Pool region and Mouyondzi district, where a 2017 ceasefire ended the conflict but clashes could recur. The FCDO advises against all travel within 50 km of the border with the Central African Republic in Likouala. Avoid walking after dark, and carry a colour copy of your passport and visa stamp, as police may ask for ID.

tips.text: Do not confuse the Republic of the Congo (Brazzaville) with the Democratic Republic of the Congo (Kinshasa) across the river: they are separate countries, each with its own visa. The UK FCDO says the Brazzaville–Kinshasa river crossing can close without warning, the ferry stops running in the late afternoon and does not run on Sundays.
The UK FCDO says you must have certificates proving yellow fever and polio vaccination to pass border control. Keep it with your passport.

Always carry identification: the UK FCDO advises a colour copy of your passport including the visa entry stamp, and the Government of Canada says you may be detained if you cannot produce acceptable identification.
The Government of Canada says the economy is primarily cash-based and that, outside major hotels and stores in Brazzaville and Pointe-Noire, credit cards are rarely accepted. Carry enough cash.

The Government of Canada says it is illegal to photograph government buildings, military installations, border crossings and transport infrastructure, including ports, train stations and airports. Ask permission before photographing official buildings or people.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for the Republic of the Congo?
faq.answer: Almost certainly yes. Apart from CEMAC citizens (Cameroon, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea, Chad and the Central African Republic), who enter freely, and Rwandans, who get a free visa on arrival, travelers must obtain a visa in advance from a Congolese embassy. No official source we found describes an electronic visa. The President has announced that citizens of all African countries will no longer need a visa from 1 January 2027.

faq.question: Can I get a visa on arrival in Congo-Brazzaville?
faq.answer: Not for most travelers. Rwandan ordinary-passport holders get a free visa on arrival for up to 90 days under a bilateral agreement; for everyone else, Canada's travel advice says a visa cannot be obtained at ports of entry, or at any Congolese embassy other than the one for your country of residence. Arrange your visa there before traveling.

faq.question: Is this the same country as the DRC?
faq.answer: No. The Republic of the Congo (capital Brazzaville) and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (capital Kinshasa) are different countries facing each other across the Congo River, each with its own visa. A visa for one is not valid for the other.

faq.question: Is yellow fever vaccination required for the Republic of the Congo?
faq.answer: Yes. The UK's travel advice says you must have a yellow fever vaccination certificate to pass border control. Keep the yellow card with your passport.

faq.question: Is the Republic of the Congo safe to visit?
faq.answer: The UK FCDO advises against all travel within 50 km of the border with the Central African Republic in Likouala Region, and warns that clashes could break out with little notice in parts of the Pool region. It reports opportunistic crime such as pickpocketing, particularly in Brazzaville and Pointe-Noire, and advises against walking after dark. Check your government’s current advice and keep identity documents on you.
